title: Synthesis of Metal-Semiconductor Heterojunctions in Single Graphene Nanoribbons
authors: Ziyi Wang, Kaitlin Slicker, Weichen Tang, Boyu Qie, Rafal Zuzak, Haowen Pang, Yudi Huang, Xinheng Li, Peter H. Jacobse, Steven G. Louie, Felix R. Fischer, Michael F. Crommie
abstract: Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) are a highly tunable class of one-dimensional (1D) quantum materials that can be fabricated through bottom-up synthesis. Precise control over GNR band gaps and band-edge alignments has established them as a promising nanoelectronics platform, but forming high-quality electronic interfaces remains challenging. Here we combine sequential on-surface synthesis and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM)-induced dehydrogenation to directly write metallic 7-iGNR segments into otherwise semiconducting H$_2$-7-iGNRs without changing the GNR width or carbon backbone connectivity. The resulting metallic segments exhibit nonzero spectral weight at the Fermi level ($E_\mathrm{F}$) and spatially extended electronic states, consistent with two dispersive bands crossing $E_\mathrm{F}$. The new metallic states are well described by an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger zigzag-ladder Hamiltonian. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) and first-principles calculations show that the valence band edge of adjacent, connected semiconducting GNR segments lies close to $E_\mathrm{F}$ for the metallic segments. STS spectra recover bulk GNR properties within $\sim$1 nm on either side of the metal-semiconductor GNR interface, with no discernible depletion region. The observed GNR band edge alignment is consistent with a small energy barrier for hole injection, thus suggesting a possible route towards atomically precise, low-barrier p-type contacts for future GNR-based electronic devices.
summary: This work reports on the synthesis and characterization of metal-semiconductor heterojunctions in single Graphene Nanoribbons. By using STM-induced dehydrogenation, the authors create metallic segments within semiconducting GNRs. The resulting junction exhibits favorable electronic alignment, suggesting a viable pathway for building atomically precise, low-barrier p-type contacts for future nanoelectronics.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the difficulty in creating high-quality, low-barrier electronic interfaces between semiconducting Graphene Nanoribbons (GNRs) and metallic contacts.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a method to synthesize metallic segments within semiconducting GNRs, creating a metal-semiconductor heterojunction with a small energy barrier for hole injection.
method: The study combines bottom-up on-surface synthesis techniques with advanced characterization using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) and Spectroscopy (STS), complemented by first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The system involves GNRs (specifically 7-iGNRs) synthesized on Au(111). The electronic structure is modeled using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) Hamiltonian and analyzed via DFT-LDA, treating the junction as a metal-semiconductor interface.
key_observables: Zero-bias conductance (nonzero spectral weight at E_F), band edge alignment, and the absence of a discernible depletion region across the interface.
important_parameters: The energy barrier for hole injection, the GNR width, and the bias voltage used for STM tip-induced dehydrogenation.
main_assumptions: The process relies on the ability to locally remove hydrogen atoms via STM tip manipulation, and STS measurements are assumed to recover bulk GNR properties near the interface.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the synthesis progression (precursor to H2-7-iGNR), the quantum ladder model, and crucially, the dI/dV spectra and LDOS maps comparing the semiconducting and metallic states across the junction.
paper_structure: The paper details the synthesis process (precursor deposition, polymerization, dehydrogenation) followed by a detailed electronic structure analysis using STS and DFT to characterize the resulting metal-semiconductor junction.
why_interesting: The precise control over electronic interfaces in 1D quantum materials like GNRs is crucial for building nanoscale electronic components, offering insights into interface physics relevant to quantum device architectures.
